## Goal

- Compute the inverse of a $2\times2$ matrix by row reduction on the augmented matrix $[\,A \mid I\,]$.
- Check your answer by confirming $A A^{-1} = I$.
- Solve a small system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ using $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$.
- Recognise a *singular* matrix that has no inverse: row reduction gives a row of zeros on the left.

## The method

The **identity matrix** $I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ is the
"1" of matrices: $A A^{-1} = I$ for any invertible $A$.

To find $A^{-1}$, write $A$ and $I$ side by side in one **augmented matrix**
$[\,A \mid I\,]$, the same shorthand as $[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$ in Linear
systems by hand, now with two columns on the right. Then use row operations
until the **left** half is $I$. The **right** half is then $A^{-1}$:

$$
[\,A \mid I\,] \;\longrightarrow\; [\,I \mid A^{-1}\,].
$$

The allowed row operations are the ones you already know:

1. Add a multiple of one row to another row (e.g. R2 $-$ 2R1).
2. Multiply a row by a nonzero number (e.g. $\tfrac12$R1).
3. Swap two rows (R1 $\leftrightarrow$ R2).

A good order for a $2\times2$: make a zero **below** the diagonal, then make
the diagonal entries $1$, then make a zero **above** the diagonal.

Every operation is done to the **whole row**, both halves. Why it works: each
row operation is the same as multiplying from the left by some matrix. When the
left half has turned from $A$ into $I$, the product of all those matrices is
$A^{-1}$, and the right half, which started as $I$, has been multiplied by
exactly that product.

**Worked example.** $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\frac12\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;2\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right]
$$

$$
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 0 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac12\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right]
$$

The left half is $I$, so
$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

Check: $A A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I.$ Correct.

**No inverse (singular).** If the columns of $A$ are parallel (one row is a
multiple of the other), row reduction produces a **row of zeros on the left**.
A zero row can never become a row of $I$, so there is no inverse. For example,
$\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,2\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 1 \end{array}\right]$:
stop here. In R, `solve()` gives an error for such a matrix.

::: {.callout-note title="Bonus shortcut (not for exam)"}
For a $2\times2$ there is also a formula, using the determinant $ad - bc$:
$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}.
$$
Swap $a$ and $d$, negate $b$ and $c$, divide every entry by $ad - bc$. If
$ad - bc = 0$ the matrix is singular. For the worked example,
$ad - bc = 2 - 1 = 1$, giving the same inverse. Bonus material: you do not need
to memorise determinants for the exam.
:::

## Drills

**Find the inverse** by row-reducing $[\,A \mid I\,]$ (all come out with simple numbers).

1. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
2. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
3. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$
4. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
5. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
6. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
7. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
8. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

**Recognise the singular matrix** (no inverse).

9. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ — does an inverse exist?
10. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ — does an inverse exist?

**Verify** $A A^{-1} = I$.

11. For drill 5, multiply $A A^{-1}$ and confirm you get $I$.
12. For drill 6, multiply $A A^{-1}$ and confirm you get $I$.

**Solve** $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ using $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$.

13. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
14. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
15. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

## Check in R

The inverse is computed by [`solve`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/solve.html) with a
single argument; the matrix product uses `%*%`. To solve $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$
directly, pass both: `solve(A, b)`.

```r
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 1), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
solve(A)
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]    1   -1
# [2,]   -1    2

A %*% solve(A)
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]    1    0
# [2,]    0    1      (the identity I)

b <- c(3, 2)
solve(A, b)
# [1] 1 1            (so x1 = 1, x2 = 1)

S <- matrix(c(1, 2,
              2, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
solve(S)
# Error: Lapack routine dgesv: system is exactly singular   (parallel columns, no inverse)
```

## Hints

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — the order of row operations"}
Start from $[\,A \mid I\,]$. (1) Make the entry below the diagonal zero
(R2 minus a multiple of R1; swap rows first if the top-left entry is $0$ or
awkward). (2) Divide each row by its diagonal entry, so the diagonal is $1$.
(3) Make the entry above the diagonal zero (R1 minus a multiple of R2). Always
apply each operation to **all four** entries of the row.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — diagonal matrices"}
For $\begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & d \end{bmatrix}$ only step (2) is needed:
multiply R1 by $1/a$ and R2 by $1/d$. The inverse is
$\begin{bmatrix} 1/a & 0 \\ 0 & 1/d \end{bmatrix}$; the off-diagonal zeros stay
zero.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — spotting a singular matrix"}
If one row of $A$ is a multiple of the other (equivalently, the columns are
parallel), subtracting that multiple gives a row of zeros on the **left**. A zero
row cannot be turned into a row of $I$: stop, there is no inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 4 — verifying the inverse"}
Row $i$ times column $j$: multiply matching entries and add. The diagonal
products should give $1$ and the off-diagonal should give $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 5 — solving with the inverse"}
$\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ is a matrix-times-vector product. Top entry of
$\mathbf{x}$ = (first row of $A^{-1}$) $\cdot \mathbf{b}$; bottom entry =
(second row) $\cdot \mathbf{b}$.
:::

## Step-by-step solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

**Drill 1.** $[\,I \mid I\,]$ is already finished: the left half is $I$, so
$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ The identity is its own
inverse.

**Drill 2.**
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac12\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac12 \end{array}\right],
\qquad
A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Drill 3.**
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac12\text{R1},\ \frac15\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & \tfrac12 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac15 \end{array}\right],
\qquad
A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{5} \end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Drill 4.** Already zero below the diagonal and $1$s on it; only the entry
above remains.
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,2\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right],
\qquad
A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Drill 5.** A shortcut first: R1 $-$ R2 gives a $1$ in the top-left corner.
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,2\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3 \end{array}\right],
$$
so $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}.$

**Drill 6.**
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 2 \end{array}\right],
$$
so $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

**Drill 7.** Swap the rows first, so the top-left entry is $1$.
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 4 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,\leftrightarrow\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,4\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & -4 \end{array}\right]
$$
$$
\xrightarrow{\;-\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 4 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 4 \end{array}\right],
$$
so $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}.$

**Drill 8.**
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,2\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & 3 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac12\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \tfrac32 \end{array}\right],
$$
so $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & \tfrac{3}{2} \end{bmatrix}.$

**Drill 9.**
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,2\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 1 \end{array}\right].
$$
The left half has a row of zeros, which can never become $(0\ 1)$. **No
inverse**: the matrix is singular (the second row is $2\times$ the first; the
columns $(1,2)$ and $(2,4)$ are parallel).

**Drill 10.**
$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,3\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 0 & 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right].
$$
A zero row on the left again: **no inverse** (the first row is $3\times$ the
second).

**Drill 11.** Using $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and
$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$:
$$
A A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
(3)(1)+(1)(-2) & (3)(-1)+(1)(3) \\
(2)(1)+(1)(-2) & (2)(-1)+(1)(3)
\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I. \checkmark
$$

**Drill 12.** Using $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and
$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$:
$$
A A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
(2)(2)+(1)(-3) & (2)(-1)+(1)(2) \\
(3)(2)+(2)(-3) & (3)(-1)+(2)(2)
\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I. \checkmark
$$

**Drill 13.** This $A$ is the worked example, so
$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. Then
$$
\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} (1)(3)+(-1)(2) \\ (-1)(3)+(2)(2) \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$
So $x_1 = 1,\ x_2 = 1$.

**Drill 14.** This $A$ is drill 4, so
$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Then
$$
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} (1)(5)+(-2)(2) \\ (0)(5)+(1)(2) \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.
$$
So $x_1 = 1,\ x_2 = 2$.

**Drill 15.** This $A$ is drill 5, so
$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Then
$$
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} (1)(4)+(-1)(3) \\ (-2)(4)+(3)(3) \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$
So $x_1 = 1,\ x_2 = 1$. (You could also row-reduce $[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$
directly, as in Linear systems by hand; the answer is the same.)

:::
